headline: Antonio Saavedra and co-authors built AMD's own proposed public-key bitstream protection into a 7-Series FPGA's fabric and then read the decrypted configuration words off its internal 32-bit port with an infrared probe, leaving every fabric-side encryption scheme stuck behind the same hard-wired interface.

items.title: Push HVPE to 1150 °C and β-Ga₂O₃ grows 14 µm an hour
items.dek: Sourav Sarker and co-authors grew β-gallium oxide — an ultra-wide-bandgap semiconductor aimed at kilovolt power switches — on native substrates by halide vapour phase epitaxy at 1150 °C, hitting 14.3 micrometres an hour and 42.9 micrometres of film in three hours.
items.why_it_matters: A vertical power device holds off voltage across a thick, lightly doped drift layer, so how many hours that layer takes to grow is a manufacturing constraint rather than a laboratory detail: forty micrometres at one micrometre an hour is a shift, and at 14.3 it is an afternoon. The orientation result is the other half of the finding — the three substrate faces answer the same recipe differently, so which face you start on now trades growth rate against the surface the next layer has to land on.
items.background_md: A vertical power diode or transistor blocks voltage across a lightly doped drift layer: thicker and purer holds off more volts, and also adds more resistance when the device is conducting. For any wide-bandgap material the engineering problem is growing that layer, and growth rate is the binding constraint, because tens of micrometres at a micrometre an hour is not a production step. Halide vapour phase epitaxy makes its metal precursor inside the reactor, by reacting HCl with a gallium source rather than delivering a metal-organic molecule from a heated vessel, and that is why it reaches rates the metal-organic routes do not.
items.deeper_md:
Growth ran on (010), (001) and (2̄01) native substrates. Raising HCl flow from 80 to 300 sccm lifts the rate up to sevenfold; 1050 → 1150 °C nearly doubles it; atmospheric pressure beats 100 Torr by more than 2.5× at 1150 °C; and cutting O₂ to 5 sccm takes the rate to 14.3 µm/h, giving films up to 42.9 µm thick in three hours.

Quality did not collapse with rate. X-ray rocking curves came out at 63.4, 66.6 and 42.8 arcsec FWHM for the (010), (001) and (2̄01) epilayers, and the (2̄01) face developed a step-and-terrace morphology with local RMS roughness as low as 0.17 nm. The orientation dependence is the mechanism to take away: one gas phase meeting three different atomic terminations gives three different step densities and incorporation paths, so the face sets morphology at least as much as the recipe does.

Nobody disputes growth rates; the contested question for β-Ga₂O₃ is electrical. This paper reports structure rather than transport — no mobility, no net doping, no deep levels — and its fastest condition is the oxygen-starved one. For scale, HVPE-grown material already holds 1.4–2.3 kV in Cr₂O₃ and NiOx heterojunction diodes at roughly 12 mΩ·cm² differential on-resistance. The material's standing handicap is untouched: first-principles work puts voltage-assisted hole concentrations in HVPE β-Ga₂O₃ near 8.7 × 10¹¹ cm⁻³, so the devices stay unipolar.

glossary.definition: Crystal growth in which the metal precursor is a halide formed inside the reactor by passing HCl over a metal source, rather than a metal-organic vapour carried in from outside.

The thick, lightly doped region a power device blocks voltage across; its thickness and doping set the breakdown voltage and contribute most of the on-resistance, so the two specifications fight each other.
The angular width of an X-ray diffraction peak as the crystal is tilted, in arcseconds; it measures how far lattice planes are misoriented across the film, so narrower means less mosaic spread.
Standard cubic centimetres per minute — a gas flow stated as the volume it would occupy at reference conditions, so it counts molecules per minute independently of chamber pressure.

items.title: A second MoS₂ layer triples the current in a sub-20 nm ribbon
items.dek: Kaichi Yamamoto, Hiroki Ago and co-authors grew aligned arrays of molybdenum disulphide nanoribbons — strips of a three-atom-thick semiconductor kept under 20 nanometres wide — one layer at a time on sapphire, and got three times the current density from bilayer ribbons as from monolayers.
items.why_it_matters: Layer count in grown two-dimensional channels has mostly been whatever the growth happened to produce, and the field's working assumption is that thinner is better, because thin is what buys gate control. Turning layer number into a dialled parameter — here by raising the molybdenum oxide supply — separates it from channel width, so a ribbon can be optimised in thickness without being made wider, and the measurement says the monolayer everyone starts from is not the best-performing option at this width.
items.background_md: A transistor fails when the gate loses electrostatic control of its channel, and the cure is a channel thinner than the length the gate has to command. One layer of a transition-metal dichalcogenide such as MoS₂ is a single metal plane between two sulphur planes, roughly 0.7 nm thick, which is why imec's logic roadmap pencils 2D channels in below the point where ultrathin silicon's mobility and drive current fall away. Shrinking the other dimension, into a ribbon tens of nanometres wide, brings the footprint down without thinning further; growing such ribbons aligned and single-crystalline is the hard part.
items.deeper_md:
The growth is chemical vapour deposition on a low-symmetry sapphire face, which is what supplies the alignment. Increasing the MoO₃ supply is what nucleates the second and later layers, and time plus supply takes the stack up to four; bilayer ribbons come out single-crystalline in 2H stacking at widths below 20 nm, and the same recipe extends to vertical MoS₂/WS₂ hetero-nanoribbons.

Averaged over devices, bilayer nanoribbon FETs show twice the carrier mobility and three times the current density of monolayer ones, with a best case of 86.7 cm²V⁻¹s⁻¹.

Two things to hold against it. 86.7 is the champion device rather than the distribution, and the quoted figure is field-effect mobility, which folds contact resistance into a number read as a material property — a live problem here, because imec names fab-compatible source/drain contacts as one of three unsolved obstacles for 2D logic, alongside depositing a dielectric onto a surface with no dangling bonds and direct growth that wants about 1000 °C. The industrial route is also not this one: ASML, TSMC and imec reached 94% working transistors at 50 nm contacted poly pitch on 300 mm wafers by EUV-patterning deposited sheets down to 28 nm channel lengths, not by growing ribbons.

glossary.definition: A layered compound of one transition metal and two chalcogen atoms, such as MoS₂, whose single layer is three atoms thick and bound to its neighbours only by van der Waals forces.
The stacking order in which each successive MoS₂ layer is rotated 180° relative to the one below, which is the arrangement bulk MoS₂ adopts naturally.
The unit of carrier mobility, here extracted from how much drain current a volt of gate swing produces; it includes contact resistance, so it is a device number rather than a material constant.
The centre-to-centre spacing from one transistor gate to the next, including its contact; it is what actually measures logic density, rather than the node name on the datasheet.

items.title: A Mott switch's reset is a bifurcation, with filament width as the knob
items.dek: Aniket Bajaj and co-authors treated switching in a vanadium dioxide device — an oxide that turns metallic once its own current has heated it enough — as a stability problem, and showed the 12.65-volt turn-on and the 1.53-volt collapse back to insulating are both saddle-node bifurcations.
items.why_it_matters: The order parameter the theory lands on is the width of the hot metallic filament, not a voltage or a resistance, and the bifurcation predicts that filament breaks off at a finite width rather than thinning continuously to nothing. That makes the reset current and the smallest reachable state properties of the device's thermal surroundings — series resistance, heat spreading into the substrate — rather than of vanadium dioxide itself, which is a different set of design knobs from the ones a materials picture offers.
items.background_md: Vanadium dioxide is an insulator that becomes a metal when heated through roughly 340 K, and in a two-terminal device the heat can come from the current itself: current warms the film, the warmer film conducts better, which draws more current. That positive feedback — thermal runaway — collapses the device into a narrow metallic filament, and it is the basis of a threshold switch, the two-terminal part used as a selector in crossbar memory and as the nonlinearity in oscillator circuits. Because the mechanism is self-heating, behaviour depends on the circuit and the heat path and not only on the material.
items.deeper_md:
The film is about 65 nm of VO₂ laid down by pulsed laser deposition at 600 °C in 10⁻² mbar of oxygen with a 248 nm KrF laser, patterned into a 10 µm × 100 µm channel between 50 nm gold electrodes on sapphire. Set: 12.65 V, with the voltage snapping down to 1.24 V and resistance falling 4500 → 350 Ω. Reset: 1.53 V, holding current about 0.6 mA, current dropping 12.7 → 1.4 mA. Ambient 330–332 K, with 1024 cycles imaged optically alongside the electrical trace.

The construction starts from the reaction–diffusion equation for heat transport, then builds Lyapunov functions that behave like Landau free energies, with the filament half-width as order parameter. Both transitions come out as saddle-node bifurcations, and the reset is first-order — break-off at finite width.

Caveats worth naming. It is mean-field with a single order parameter, and the predicted critical half-width is left as a function of load resistance and thermal parameters rather than a number. More awkwardly, the cycling data show an initial electro-spatial forming phase before a stable stochastic regime — which is the non-volatile, defect-migration effect other groups put at the centre of VO₂ switching, and the same chemical inhomogeneity that lets mixed vanadium oxides switch at threshold fields about 100× lower than stoichiometric VO₂. The clean bifurcation picture describes the formed device, not a virgin one.

glossary.definition: The abrupt change in a correlated oxide from insulating to metallic conduction — near 340 K in VO₂ — triggered here by the device heating itself rather than by an oven.
The point where a stable and an unstable solution of a dynamical system collide and vanish, leaving no nearby state to sit in; it is what makes a switching event abrupt instead of gradual.
The single quantity whose value distinguishes two phases in a Landau-style description; here it is the width of the metallic filament, not anything about the crystal structure.
A region where more current means less voltage across the device, so it cannot be held stably from a voltage source — the set event lands at 1.24 V from 12.65 V.

items.title: Strip two hydrogens and the graphene ribbon becomes its own contact
items.dek: Michael Crommie and Felix Fischer's groups used a scanning tunnelling microscope tip to pull hydrogen off short stretches of a semiconducting graphene nanoribbon, turning those stretches metallic without altering the ribbon's width or carbon backbone, and found no depletion region at the junctions that result.
items.why_it_matters: Getting carriers into a one-nanometre-wide channel is what has limited bottom-up graphene ribbon transistors: landing a metal on the ribbon leaves a Schottky barrier the carriers must tunnel through, and that barrier is what capped the best such devices near a microamp. A contact made of the same ribbon in a different hydrogenation state has no second material to misalign, and the spectra recover bulk behaviour within about a nanometre of the interface, so the contact costs almost no length.
items.background_md: Carriers have to get from a metal wire into a semiconductor channel, and at that junction the two materials' energy levels generally do not line up. A Schottky barrier forms, and the semiconductor surrenders a depletion region — a stretch emptied of mobile carriers — to screen the difference. Depletion width grows as doping falls, so in an undoped channel a few nanometres across the depleted stretch can be longer than the device, which is why contact resistance rather than channel transport limits most one- and two-dimensional transistors. Graphene nanoribbons are assembled molecule by molecule on a surface, so width and edge shape fix the bandgap exactly.
items.deeper_md:
Sequential on-surface synthesis builds the semiconducting ribbon, H₂-7-iGNR; STM-induced dehydrogenation then writes metallic 7-iGNR segments into it, leaving width and carbon connectivity untouched, so the only thing that changed is which hydrogens are present. The metallic segments carry nonzero spectral weight at the Fermi level and spatially extended states consistent with two dispersive bands crossing it, and an extended Su–Schrieffer–Heeger zigzag-ladder Hamiltonian reproduces them.

The interface is the result. Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy and first-principles calculation put the adjacent semiconducting segment's valence band edge close to the metallic segment's Fermi level, and the spectra recover bulk ribbon properties within about 1 nm either side, with no discernible depletion region — consistent with a small barrier for hole injection.

The limits are large and the authors state them. This is one ribbon at a time, written by a tip, on a surface, measured by STM: nothing has been transferred to an insulator, nothing contacted by an electrode, and the small hole barrier is inferred from band alignment rather than measured as a contact resistance. The same groups' earlier route to metallic ribbons inserted a superlattice of zero-energy modes during synthesis, which means choosing a different starting molecule; dehydrogenation edits the finished ribbon in place. For scale, 9-atom-wide armchair ribbon FETs with a 20 nm channel and a thin high-k gate reached I_on above 1 µA at V_d = −1 V with I_on/I_off around 10⁵, and concluded that Schottky-barrier tunnelling set the ceiling.

glossary.definition: The stretch of semiconductor beside a junction emptied of mobile carriers to screen the built-in field; its width rises as doping falls, so undoped nanomaterials give very wide ones.
The energy at which an electronic state is half occupied; a contact injects easily when the semiconductor's band edge sits near the metal's E_F, because there is then little barrier to climb.
Measuring tunnelling current against tip voltage at a single point, which returns the local density of electronic states at that atom-scale position rather than an average.
A one-dimensional tight-binding chain with alternating strong and weak bonds — the minimal model for a conjugated carbon chain, and the standard account of its end states.

items.title: Remap the logic after placement, not before, and the critical path moves
items.dek: Zijian Jiang, Keren Zhu and co-authors re-ran technology mapping — the step that picks which library cells implement a circuit — after placement instead of before, inside bounded windows around critical paths, and cut geometric-mean worst negative slack 86.7% against the previous best remapper across nine benchmark designs.
items.why_it_matters: In the standard flow, mapping commits to gate choices using a wire-load estimate made before anything has coordinates, and placement then invalidates the delay model that justified those choices. Closing that loop with estimated locations and routing-based parasitics recovered most of the slack on critical paths without touching the source or the library, and it came with lower area on every design — which inverts the timing-for-area trade that buffer insertion and upsizing normally force.
items.background_md: A digital chip is compiled. Synthesis turns a hardware description into a netlist of generic gates; technology mapping chooses which cells from a standard-cell library actually implement that netlist; placement decides where each cell physically sits; routing wires them together. The ordering is the problem, because mapping has to guess wire length before anything has coordinates, and at advanced nodes the resistance and capacitance of the wiring is a large share of path delay. Static timing analysis then scores the result, reporting the worst violating path on the design and the sum of every violation.
items.deeper_md:
Timing-critical regions are cut out as bounded windows whose interfaces retain the surrounding circuit's constraints and fanout loads. Inside each window a mixed-integer formulation jointly selects logic cuts, signal polarities and library cells under a delay model fed by estimated locations and interconnect parasitics; a continuous relaxation prunes the space before the discrete solve emits several implementations with similar modelled timing and different structure. Each candidate is legalised, routed for parasitic estimation and re-timed, and only the physically validated ones go back into the design, updating the context the next window sees.

Numbers, on 2024 ICCAD Contest Problem C and 2025 MLCAD Contest designs in ASAP7 with OpenROAD as the physical backend. Against PigMap3 across nine designs: better WNS on seven and better TNS on eight, geometric-mean violation magnitudes down 86.7% and 95.2%, and lower area on all nine. Under a uniform flow against annealing and genetic baselines on seven designs: 48.6–49.2% WNS and 53.3–63.1% TNS reductions. Budget: at most 20 windows inside max(1800, ⌈2t_ref + 600⌉) seconds.

The caveat is in how the headline is computed. A percentage cut in violation magnitude flatters a design that was nearly closed already, and a win counted on seven of nine treats a path at −1 ps the same as one at −100 ps. These are contest benchmarks on a predictive academic library and an academic backend, not a foundry kit with a foundry signoff tool.

glossary.definition: The compiler step that covers a generic logic network with cells that exist in the target library, choosing among functionally identical implementations with different delay, area and drive strength.
Slack is how much earlier a signal arrives than it must; WNS is the single worst violating path, TNS the sum over all of them — one says whether it fails, the other how much work is left.
The resistance and capacitance of the wiring itself, extracted from routed geometry; at a 7 nm-class library these dominate path delay, so a delay model without them is a guess.
An open 7 nm predictive FinFET process design kit from Arizona State University and Arm Research, used in research because real foundry kits are under non-disclosure.

items.fab_angle: For anyone closing timing on a cell-based design, the usable message is that the knob to reach for after placement is not only drive strength and buffering but the gate choice itself — a different cut of the same logic, re-legalised and re-timed where it actually sits. The whole flow here runs on OpenROAD and ASAP7, both free, so the experiment is reproducible by a student team rather than only inside a vendor tool.

items.title: An infrared probe reads the bitstream the FPGA just decrypted
items.dek: Antonio Saavedra and co-authors implemented AMD's own proposed public-key scheme for protecting an FPGA's configuration file inside the chip's programmable logic, then recovered decrypted configuration words anyway by shining a 1300-nanometre laser through the back of the die at the internal configuration bus.
items.why_it_matters: Moving bitstream decryption up into the fabric was meant to escape the hard-wired schemes that have already been broken and cannot be patched; this says the escape route funnels through the same hard-wired port. Whatever the cryptography, the fabric must hand plaintext configuration frames to the configuration engine over a fixed 32-bit bus whose physical position is identical on every device of that part number, so the remaining defences are physical and temporal rather than cryptographic.
items.background_md: An FPGA contains no circuit until it is configured: a bitstream sets millions of routing switches and lookup-table contents, so that file is the design — an attacker who reads it holds the netlist, and one who edits it can insert hardware. Decryption has to happen inside the device, which means plaintext frames exist on an internal bus at some moment. Separately, silicon stops absorbing light beyond about 1.1 µm, so failure-analysis labs read switching nodes from the back of a die with infrared probes, contactlessly, straight through the substrate.
items.deeper_md:
The target is an AMD XC7A200T Artix-7, a 28 nm part in a lidless flip-chip SBG484 package, which gives backside access with no delidding. The instrument is a PHEMOS-1000 with an InGaAs camera and a 1300 nm source: photon-emission microscopy locates the activity first, then electro-optical probing reads it. ICAP, the internal configuration access port, is 32 bits wide, clocked up to 100 MHz, and physically laid out as an 8×4 array of bit positions — which is what makes it addressable optically at all.

Their proof-of-concept protection is RSA-768 or RSA-1024 key transport with AES-256-CBC, built in the programmable logic: 34,908 LUTs (25%) and 33,361 flip-flops (12%) for the static design, plus 30,691 LUTs and 20,434 flip-flops for key generation. From the probed bus they recovered plaintext words matching known Vivado-generated bitstream headers, including the synchronisation word and command register values.

The bound they state themselves is the caveat: roughly four hours of averaging per probed block, against a full configuration that takes about 50 seconds over a 921,600-baud link, so recovering a whole bitstream this way would take years. This is evidence that the leak exists and is localised, not a cloning attack. It lands on a family where Starbleed already achieved a full break by using the FPGA as a decryption oracle through the same interface. The countermeasures proposed are accordingly physical: jitter the ICAP clock, delay writes randomly, write frames out of order via the FAR register, coat the backside.

glossary.definition: The configuration file that defines an FPGA's function by setting every routing switch and lookup-table bit; it is the design, so reading it is cloning and writing it is implantation.

The internal configuration access port — a hard-wired 32-bit interface through which logic running inside the FPGA writes configuration frames to the configuration engine. It cannot be bypassed or redesigned.

Reflecting an infrared laser off a transistor from the back of the die and reading the modulation its switching imposes on the returned light, which recovers the node's value with no electrical contact.
Rewriting part of an FPGA's fabric while the rest keeps running; it is what allows a design to implement its own bitstream-decryption scheme instead of trusting the hard-wired one.

items.title: Round stochastically in the MLP, to nearest at the output head
items.dek: Yohan Chatelain and Pablo de Oliveira Castro held the number format fixed and varied only the rounding rule, operation by operation, inside a small GPT-2: at six significand bits, stochastic rounding in the feed-forward block left perplexity at 1.15× the full-precision value where round-to-nearest left 2.21×.
items.why_it_matters: Low-precision inference is normally specified as a format per tensor, which treats rounding as a property of the hardware rather than a choice. This says the rule is an independent knob that has to be assigned per site, because what matters is not the size of the rounding error but what the output softmax does with it: an error that shifts every logit equally is invisible, and one that varies across the vocabulary is not. Assigning both rules by site landed within 1.10×.
items.background_md: Any floating-point result that does not fit the format has to be rounded, and the default rule, round-to-nearest, is deterministic and therefore biased — an identical value is always pushed the same direction. Accumulate that over a long sum, and the inner product inside a matrix multiply is one, and the errors add up roughly linearly in the number of terms. Stochastic rounding instead goes up or down at random, with probability set by how close the value sits to each neighbour, which makes the error zero-mean so it accumulates as a random walk. The price is variance in place of bias.
items.deeper_md:
The tooling is a variable-precision stochastic rounding algorithm that extends the PRISM backend of Verificarlo — which instruments a program at compile time and rounds every floating-point operation to a virtual precision chosen at run time — to arbitrary precisions, with a proof that the rounding decision itself is evaluated exactly in hardware floating point.

Two analyses explain the site dependence. A probabilistic forward-error bound for linear projections gives stochastic rounding an envelope growing as O(√n·u) in reduction length n against O(n·u) for round-to-nearest, a gap that widens at low precision and is widest in the long MLP down-projection. Then a second-order decomposition of the expected cross-entropy change at the output softmax splits into signed drift, drift curvature and a Fisher-weighted variance penalty: MLP noise is predominantly a uniform logit shift, which softmax ignores, so the added variance is largely discounted, while head noise is non-uniform across the vocabulary and is not.

Measured on DistilGPT-2 at six significand bits: 1.15× versus 2.21× perplexity for the MLP site, the ordering reversed at the language-model head, and 1.10× for the mixed assignment, a 28% reduction over matched-bit round-to-nearest. The caveats are the model and the method — six transformer layers, arithmetic emulated rather than executed on hardware that implements stochastic rounding, and perplexity as the only reported metric. The identified head mechanism is non-uniformity across the vocabulary, so the size of that effect should depend on vocabulary size, which a single model cannot test.

glossary.definition: Half the gap between 1 and the next representable number in a format — the relative error a single rounding can introduce, which is why error bounds are written as multiples of u.
The bits of a floating-point number that carry its digits, as distinct from its exponent; six of them sits well below FP16's ten, which is why the rounding rule becomes visible at all.
The exponential of a language model's average per-token cross-entropy; quoting it as a ratio to the full-precision value states what a numerical change costs in predictive quality.
Adding the same constant to every logit leaves the softmax probabilities unchanged, which is why an error uniform across the vocabulary is free and a non-uniform one is not.

foundations.topic: Precursors, gases, and the specialty chemical supply chain
foundations.subtitle: A deposition recipe is also a shopping list: what makes a molecule usable in a reactor, and what happens when the world has one route to a gas.
foundations.tldr: Every film in a chip arrives as a gas or a vapour, and the molecule carrying the atom you want has to satisfy a short and unforgiving list: volatile enough to move, stable enough to survive the trip, reactive enough to stick — and then stop. That list is restrictive enough that for several important layers there is effectively one molecule in use, and for one gas, effectively one production route on the planet. The chemistry is the reason; the supply fragility follows from it.

sections.heading: The spec sheet a precursor has to pass
sections.body_md: Start from the constraint: you cannot deposit an atom you cannot get to the wafer. Delivery is by vapour, so the first number on any precursor datasheet is vapour pressure, and atomic-layer-deposition practice wants more than 0.1 Torr at whatever temperature you are willing to heat the vessel to. Below that you cannot push enough molecules down the line to cover a wafer inside a pulse short enough to be useful. Heating the vessel raises vapour pressure, which collides immediately with the second requirement: the molecule has to be thermally stable, in the delivery line and on a hot wafer, because a precursor that falls apart on its own has stopped being self-limiting and become ordinary CVD. The gap between those two temperatures is the process window, and it can be narrow. Titanium is the worked example — Ti(OMe)₄ holds together to about 350 °C where Ti(OiPr)₄ does not, and that difference alone is reason enough to pick one.
sections.deeper_md: The third requirement is the one that is easiest to state and hardest to satisfy: sufficient reactivity with the surface groups that are actually present. A precursor that is volatile and stable but unreactive toward a hydroxyl-terminated oxide will simply not nucleate, which is the standard failure when a recipe developed on one underlayer is moved to another. This is also why area-selective deposition works at all: the same molecule can be reactive on one termination and inert on another, so blocking the surface chemistry — rather than masking it lithographically — becomes a patterning method.

sections.heading: Why one cycle does not give you one layer
sections.body_md: What makes ALD different from CVD is that the surface reaction runs out of places to go. A precursor pulse chemisorbs until the available sites are taken, and after that more precursor changes nothing: dose for twice as long and you get the same thickness. That is the self-limiting step, and it is a property of the chemistry rather than a setting on the tool — which is why you cannot make an arbitrary CVD precursor behave like an ALD one by shortening the pulse. The surprise is that saturation almost never delivers a full monolayer. The precursor lands with its organic ligands still attached, and those groups physically occupy the space over neighbouring sites, so the layer is sparse by construction. Trimethylaluminium and water, the most-run ALD process in existence, gives 1.0 to 1.1 Å per cycle, comfortably under an Al₂O₃ monolayer. Ligand bulk is the lever, and it is chosen long before the tool is bought.
sections.deeper_md: Two distinct effects cap growth per cycle and they are worth separating, because they respond differently. Steric hindrance is geometric: the ligand's footprint blocks adjacent sites, so growth per cycle scales roughly with the inverse of the ligand's cross-section, and swapping to a smaller ligand raises it. A limited number of active sites is chemical: the surface simply does not present enough reactive groups, and the fix is a surface treatment or a different co-reactant rather than a different ligand. Confusing the two is how a process gets optimised in the wrong direction for a quarter.

sections.heading: The precursor writes its own impurities into the film
sections.body_md: Whatever the metal arrives attached to has to leave, and some of it does not. Metal halides are attractive precursors — small, volatile, cheap, thermally robust — and they bring a halogen into the reactor with every dose. Hafnium tetrachloride deposition at 225 °C leaves roughly 5% chlorine behind in the film, and chlorine in a gate dielectric is a fixed charge, a mobile ion and a reliability problem at once. Raising the temperature drives the residue down, but the thermal budget is already committed to things upstream, so the usual answer is to change molecules rather than conditions: pick a metal-organic whose ligands leave as volatile organics instead. That buys lower halogen residue and costs you elsewhere, because the replacement molecule is bigger, less thermally stable and more expensive. There is no clean choice here, only a traded one, and that trade is why a single material can have half a dozen competing precursors in production at once.
sections.deeper_md: Notice what this does to a qualification schedule. The impurity level is a function of deposition temperature, so a film qualified at 300 °C is not the same film at 250 °C even with an identical recipe and an identical tool. Any process change that lowers the thermal budget — a temperature-sensitive underlayer, a low-k dielectric already in place, a device layer above the first one — reopens the precursor choice, not just the recipe. This is one of the quieter reasons monolithic 3D integration is hard: the 400 °C ceiling does not merely slow deposition down, it disqualifies molecules.

sections.heading: Tungsten, and the fluorine you have to spend
sections.body_md: Tungsten fills the contacts and vias that connect transistors up to the first metal layer, and it arrives as tungsten hexafluoride: six fluorine atoms per tungsten, all of which have to go somewhere. In one AMD process description the wafer sits at 395 to 460 °C — advantageously 445 °C — under 30 to 50 Torr, with WF₆ at 350 to 500 sccm and hydrogen at 6,000 to 8,000 sccm, while silane is dosed at two levels, 30 to 40 sccm to start the nucleation and 15 to 20 sccm afterwards. Both the hydrogen and the silane reduce the WF₆, depositing tungsten and liberating fluorine. Most of that fluorine finds hydrogen, becomes HF and is pumped away. The fraction that does not is the entire reason the nucleation step exists: fluorine reaching the titanium adhesion layer underneath forms TiFₓ, which degrades the barrier's resistivity and can end in the stack delaminating. That first thin tungsten film is a sacrificial shield.
sections.deeper_md: The two-level silane scheme in that patent is a dosing argument rather than a chemistry one. A higher initial silane flow gets a continuous tungsten film down fast, which is what shields the barrier; a lower flow afterwards continues nucleation without the silicon incorporation and roughness that sustained silane-rich conditions produce. The general shape recurs across the industry: when a precursor brings along an element that attacks something underneath, the first few nanometres of the film are deposited under conditions chosen for protection, and only then does the recipe switch to conditions chosen for the film's actual properties — resistivity, grain size, stress.

sections.heading: Neon is not mined, it is skimmed
sections.body_md: Neon is not produced; it is recovered. It comes off a cryogenic air separation unit — a plant whose actual business is making oxygen and nitrogen — as part of the fraction that refuses to liquefy when everything else does. In Praxair's description of the recovery, nitrogen-rich shelf vapour from the high-pressure column and a stream of liquid nitrogen condensate are fed to a stripping column for non-condensables, whose overhead gas is rich in neon; the simulated crude stream runs 51.89% neon and 15.25% helium, with better than 95% of the neon recovered, and it then goes to a separate refinery to have the helium and hydrogen taken out. Read that process backwards and the supply curve falls out. Neon output is set by how much air the world is separating for other reasons, at plants built and sited for oxygen demand. Wanting more neon does not make more neon; it bids for somebody else's by-product.
sections.deeper_md: The structural point is that the marginal cost curve is almost vertical in the short run. An air separation unit sized for an oxygen contract produces a fixed trickle of non-condensables whatever the neon price does, and adding a recovery train to a plant that lacks one is a capital project measured in years, not a response to a spot market. That is a different supply shape from a mined commodity, where price eventually calls out marginal production. It is also why a neon buyer's real exposure is not to the gas market but to the industrial geography of steel and chemicals, which is where large air separation units get built.

sections.heading: What single-sourcing costs: run the substitution test
sections.body_md: The way to make a supply dependency concrete is to ask what the substitute costs you, in the units of the process. Take neon's largest semiconductor use: it is the buffer gas, the overwhelming majority of the mixture, in the argon-fluoride excimer lasers that print at 193 nm. Helium is the obvious stand-in, cheaper and separated from natural gas rather than from air. BOC's patent on excimer gas mixtures puts the penalty plainly: a pure helium buffer yields only 60 to 70% of the power achieved with a pure neon buffer. It also gives the compromise, which is the interesting part — a buffer of 5 to 50% helium with the balance neon works, preferably 5 to 30%, and at 20% helium the output power is substantially the same as with pure neon. That is the real shape of a single-source dependency. A partial substitute exists, going all the way costs you a third of your light, and the blend that actually works still needs four-fifths neon.
sections.deeper_md: Run the same test on the other gases in this piece and the answers differ sharply, which is the practical lesson. Tungsten hexafluoride has no substitute at all for the same film — the fluorine is how the molecule is volatile — so the mitigation is inventory and multiple suppliers of the same molecule. Trimethylaluminium has several substitutes, including non-pyrophoric liquid alternatives, at a growth-rate and cost penalty you can measure in Å per cycle. Neon sits in between: substitutable in part, at a quantified power cost, with the blend still exposed to the by-product supply. Three gases, three completely different risk postures, and a procurement plan that treats them the same is wrong about two of them.

glossary.definition: The molecule that carries the atom you want to deposit. It is chosen for how it behaves in transit and on the surface — volatility, thermal stability, reactivity — rather than for the element inside it.

The pressure of a substance's own vapour above its condensed phase at a given temperature. ALD practice asks for more than 0.1 Torr, because below that you cannot move enough molecules to saturate a wafer in a usable pulse time.

A heated vessel of liquid or solid precursor through which a carrier gas is passed so that it leaves saturated with precursor vapour. The vessel temperature sets the dose, which is why vapour pressure is the first line on the datasheet.

The thickness ALD adds per complete precursor-plus-co-reactant cycle. It is usually a fraction of a monolayer, because the precursor's own ligands crowd out neighbouring surface sites; TMA and water give 1.0–1.1 Å.

The crowding of a surface by organic groups still attached to a chemisorbed precursor, which blocks adjacent reaction sites and caps growth below one monolayer per cycle. Distinct from simply running out of reactive sites.

The gases in an air separation unit that remain vapour when nitrogen and oxygen have liquefied — neon, helium, hydrogen. This stream is where neon is captured, which is why neon output tracks oxygen demand.
The majority component of an excimer laser's gas mixture. It does not itself lase, but it sets the discharge and energy-transfer conditions, so substituting it changes the laser's output power.

foundations.try_this: Open Li, Chai and Wang's ALD review — it is open access — and read the precursor-requirements section, then do two things with it. First, take the trimethylaluminium/water growth rate it quotes, 1.0–1.1 Å per cycle, and work out how many cycles and how many hours a 20 nm film needs at one second per half-cycle; that arithmetic is the whole reason ALD is used for thin layers and never for thick ones. Second, pull the safety data sheet for whichever precursor or process gas is actually on the shelf in the teaching cleanroom and find its vapour-pressure line. If it is under 0.1 Torr at room temperature, you now know why the vessel has a heater on it, and roughly how hot that heater has to get.
